title: Quit Social Media
coreMove: Judge each network tool by whether its concrete benefits substantially outweigh the attention it costs.
sourcePressure: The source frame says to use a craftsman mindset and keep only tools that substantially support what matters.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says social media is distracting; the chapter must teach a cost-benefit tool test tied to real values and outcomes.

counterintuition: some useful tools are still not worth it

exampleSpecs.domain: a freelance cartographer evaluating a professional mapping forum
exampleSpecs.audience: a specialist who gets occasional leads from an online network
exampleSpecs.stakes: attention spent browsing weak threads may crowd out portfolio map production
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she lists the two jobs the forum actually produced, compares them with the lost drafting hours, and decides whether the tool substantially supports her craft
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a half-rendered trail map beside a forum thread with twenty unread replies

exampleSpecs.domain: a community theater director using event platforms for auditions
exampleSpecs.audience: an organizer whose tool has one real benefit and many tempting side paths
exampleSpecs.stakes: casting suffers if outreach is weak, but rehearsal prep suffers if browsing expands
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he keeps the event-listing function but drops the feed habit after matching each feature to audition turnout
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an audition sign-up sheet beside an event dashboard

exampleSpecs.domain: a rural veterinarian deciding whether a short-video channel helps client education
exampleSpecs.audience: a practitioner weighing reach against attention cost
exampleSpecs.stakes: farm calls and medical notes slip if content creation becomes a second job
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she reviews a month of appointment outcomes and sees which videos changed client behavior versus which only collected views
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a clinic appointment ledger beside a phone mounted on a small tripod

exampleSpecs.domain: a labor organizer evaluating group chats across three worksites
exampleSpecs.audience: an organizer whose values include trust, turnout, and worker safety
exampleSpecs.stakes: the wrong tool leaks energy into chatter without building turnout
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he maps each chat to actual turnout actions and cuts the channel that produces noise without reliable commitments
exampleSpecs.firstImage: three group-chat names written beside a turnout tally sheet

exampleSpecs.domain: a ceramicist selling limited kiln openings online
exampleSpecs.audience: a solo craft business owner deciding whether a platform deserves daily attention
exampleSpecs.stakes: custom orders matter, but glaze testing is the scarce work
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she asks which platform activity directly sells kiln slots, then removes the features that only create comparison and browsing
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a kiln schedule card beside a platform analytics page

exampleSpecs.domain: a public defender using a professional listserv
exampleSpecs.audience: a lawyer whose network tool can either save research time or become a reflex
exampleSpecs.stakes: client motions need legal substance more than constant thread monitoring
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she keeps the digest that surfaces rare motion examples and cancels real-time alerts that fracture writing blocks
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a motion draft with a listserv digest printed beside it

skillTargets: apply the craftsman mindset to network tools
distinguish any benefit from substantial support
choose limited use rather than blanket deletion when justified

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one network tool and write the exact valuable outcome it produced in the last month, then write the attention cost beside it.
